npmatch: The Training & Evaluation Dataset

Source: vignettes/training-dataset.qmd

A hand-labeled benchmark of 1,502 organizations linking the SAM/USASpending nonprofit registry to the IRS Business Master File — how it was built, how the matcher performs on it, and how to use it to train and benchmark Stage-1 classifiers or drive an LLM review loop.

1. What this dataset is

npmatch links organizations that appear as nonprofits in the SAM / USASpending registry (keyed by UEI) to the IRS Business Master File of exempt organizations (keyed by EIN). To measure and improve that process we hand-labeled a benchmark of 1,502 source organizations:

  • 1,000 a true random sample of SAM nonprofits — use these for population performance and outcome-class prevalence.
  • 502 hard cases — an oversample of the difficult residual (fuzzy names, DBA/address divergence, ambiguous entities). Use these to probe failure modes and train a classifier on the cases that actually matter; do not read population rates off this stratum.

The benchmark does triple duty: a validation set for the matcher, a training set for Stage-1 (name/address) classifier models, and a demo corpus for exploring the package.

2. How the dataset was built

  1. Source. SAM’s public monthly extract, filtered to nonprofit business-type codes (np_flag_nonprofits(); codes A8/BZ/2U/A7) — roughly 165,000 organizations.
  2. Sample. A 1,000-org random draw plus a 502-org oversample of hard residual cases, each tagged with sample_type.
  3. Match. The shipped cascade (np_cascade()) against the unified BMF (active + inactive, 3.69M records), producing a YES/MAYBE/NO tier and scored candidates for every org.
  4. Ground truth. Each case was adjudicated with a mix of algorithmic agreement, human review, LLM judgment, and web verification — confirming that accepted matches are correct, and (crucially) investigating whether non-matches are truly not nonprofits or simply missing from the BMF.

Each org is assigned one outcome class:

Outcome class Meaning
in_bmf_match A correct BMF EIN exists (active or inactive).
nonprofit_not_in_bmf A real nonprofit with no BMF record (many churches, lapsed orgs, state-only registrations).
not_a_nonprofit Not actually a nonprofit — a SAM mislabel (for-profit, government unit).
no_match_or_na No match and not clearly classifiable as the above.
cant_determine Insufficient evidence to decide.

The inactive-BMF correction

An important labeling subtlety: matching uses the unified BMF (active + inactive) on purpose. 30 organizations first tagged “not in BMF” — because labeling initially checked only the active file — turned out to be exact name + address matches to inactive BMF records (lapsed or recently-registered orgs). These were corrected to in_bmf_match with the inactive EIN (20 by an exact name+address rule, 10 confirmed on manual/web review). A further 6 plausible-but-unconfirmed candidates were reviewed and rejected (affiliate siblings such as a hospital’s Foundation, and cross-state name collisions). The gt_notes column records every such decision.

3. Record-linkage performance

The positive event is a correct EIN link. Recall = correct links ÷ linkable orgs; precision = correct ÷ accepted; the MAYBE tier is a human/LLM review queue, not an error bucket.

Metric Random (n=1,000) Hard (n=502) All (n=1,502)
Linkable orgs 807 380 1,187
Non-linkable orgs 193 122 315
Recall — auto (YES only) 88.1% 70.0% 82.3%
Recall — auto + review 95.0% 86.1% 92.2%
Precision (YES picks correct) 99.2% 96.0% 98.3%
Auto-accept false positives 5 7 12

Read the random column as expected real-world performance: ~95% of linkable nonprofits are recovered once the review tier is worked, at ~99% precision on the auto-accepted matches. The hard column is the deliberately-difficult residual.

Algorithm-only tiering (before any review):

Tier Random Hard Meaning
YES (auto-accept) 717 277 strong name + address, no veto
MAYBE (review) 123 136 surfaced for human/LLM confirmation
NO (withhold) 144 87 nothing cleared the review floor
No candidates 16 2 blocking found nothing

Because some organizations are legitimately unmatchable, the match rate must be read against how often a match can exist. From the representative random sample:

Outcome class Random Share
in BMF (matchable) 807 80.7%
nonprofit, not in BMF 85 8.5%
not a nonprofit (SAM mislabel) 65 6.5%
no match / n.a. 22 2.2%
can’t determine 21 2.1%

So ~81% of SAM “nonprofit” registrations are matchable to the BMF; the ~19% remainder are correctly not matched — and a NO here can be a true negative (the record is not in fact a nonprofit), not a failed match. Two denominators therefore matter: recall among the linkable 81%** (95%), and yield over the whole population** (~77% of all source orgs receive a correct link).

4. The dataset files

File Grain Rows Description
EVAL-FRAME-1502-MERGED.csv candidate pair 2,763 Reviewable evaluation frame (150 cols) + ground truth.
GROUNDTRUTH-MASTER-1502.csv source org 1,502 One row per org: the archival label key.
TRAINING-PAIRS-1502.csv candidate pair 304,274 Model-training projection: features + label per scored pair.
DATA-DICTIONARY-EVAL-FRAME.md / .csv — 150 Column dictionary for the evaluation frame.

The three data frames are three views of the same run: the ground-truth master is the label key; the evaluation frame joins those labels onto the reviewable top candidates; the training pairs are a projection of every scored candidate (features + a boolean label).

5. Benchmarking Stage-1 classifiers

TRAINING-PAIRS-1502.csv is one row per scored candidate pair with a boolean label (1 = this EIN is the true match) and the comparison features the scorers calibrate on: the continuous field similarities name_sim, street_sim, city_sim, zip_sim (Jaro-Winkler / agreement, 0–1), the binary geographic-agreement flags geo_stnum/geo_zip9/geo_zip5/geo_zip3/ geo_state/geo_pobox, the categorical name_match_type, the name distinctiveness name_freq, and the current blended score. It is exactly the input to the package’s model tools:

library(npmatch)
path  <- np_fetch("https://<archive>/TRAINING-PAIRS-1502.csv")   # fetch-only (too large to bundle)
pairs <- read.csv(path)

# cross-validated comparison of weighted / EM (reclin2) / model scorers
np_benchmark(pairs, methods = c("weighted", "em", "model"),
             target_precision = 0.98, min_recall = 0.95)

# fit a single Stage-1 model on the field-similarity features
fit <- np_train(pairs, engine = "logit",
                features = c("name_sim", "street_sim", "city_sim", "zip_sim",
                             "geo_stnum", "geo_zip9", "geo_zip5", "geo_state", "geo_pobox"))

# score quality + a precision-first operating point
np_auc(pairs$score, pairs$label)
np_tune_thresholds(pairs$score, pairs$label,
                   target_precision = 0.98, min_recall = 0.95)

On this benchmark the geography-adaptive hier scorer is the shipped default (it beat a cross-validated GLM at scale); the training pairs let you reproduce that comparison or fit your own Stage-1 classifier.

6. What the evaluation dataframe looks like

EVAL-FRAME-1502-MERGED.csv is candidate-level: one row per (source org × BMF candidate). Group by uei to see an org’s competing candidates. Two flags orient every group:

  • is_top_candidate = 1 — the algorithm’s chosen pick.
  • is_gt_ein = 1 — the row whose EIN is the ground-truth correct match.

Alongside the similarity features it carries the full evidence a reviewer needs: normalized name variants (name_*_normalized), IDF-annotated tokens (name_*_tokenized), geographic agreement flags (geo_*), the veto trail (veto*), and imported BMF context (BMF_ntee_clean, BMF_subsection, BMF_form_990, …) and SAM context (SAM_bus_type_*). All 150 columns are documented in DATA-DICTIONARY-EVAL-FRAME.md. This is the frame the candidate-evaluation-frame vignette describes field by field.

7. From MAYBE to an LLM review loop

The MAYBE tier is where the algorithm defers to judgment. np_route() turns a cascade result into a review packet, and np_as_prompt() / np_as_prompts() render each MAYBE case as a self-contained LLM adjudication prompt — the source org, its candidate BMF entities with fields and similarities, why it was flagged, and a JSON-output instruction:

routing <- np_route(res, bmf = bmf_raw, sam = sam_raw)   # res = np_cascade() result
prompts <- np_as_prompts(routing)                        # one prompt per review case

# deploy: send each prompt to your LLM, collect {ein, decision, confidence, reason}
for (id in names(prompts)) {
  verdict <- my_llm(prompts[[id]])                       # your model call
  # ...record verdict, promote confirmed matches, drop rejected ones
}

The same packet drives a human reviewer or an LLM — the prompt is just formatted text, so the second-stage process is model-agnostic and easy to deploy. This is the two-stage philosophy in practice: the algorithm surfaces and sorts; a human or LLM confirms the uncertain middle.

8. Loading the data

The evaluation frame and the ground-truth master ship with the package and lazy-load by name. The full training pairs (304k rows) are too large to bundle, so they are fetched from the shared data archive on demand.

data("npmatch_eval")          # candidate-level evaluation frame + ground truth (2,763 x 150)
data("npmatch_groundtruth")   # query-level labels (1,502 x 17)

# full training pairs: fetch from the shared archive
path  <- np_fetch("https://<archive>/TRAINING-PAIRS-1502.csv")
pairs <- read.csv(path)
